html: Reinforcement learning (RL) is becoming increasingly important for post-training robot policies: by continually interacting with the environment, a policy can improve beyond the ceiling imposed by behavior cloning. However, robot interaction is expensive, and training often relies on sparse terminal outcomes that provide little information about which actions caused success or failure, leading to inefficient or unstable optimization. Obtaining dense process-level supervision is therefore a central challenge. Inspired by inverse reinforcement learning and built on Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), we propose Group Teaching Policy Optimization (GTPO). Within each group of rollouts from the same initial configuration, GTPO represents every rollout as a trajectory of visual features, pairs each failure with its nearest successful rollout as an on-policy teacher, and uses temporal optimal transport to convert the sparse trajectory-level signal into dense chunk-level credit. A temporal mask restricts distant matches during alignment, while the in-group teacher improves together with the policy. OT teaching requires no additional expert reference trajectories or reward model. On all four LIBERO suites, GTPO reaches 98.65% average success from a one-demonstration-per-task warm start and 99.70% with the full demonstration set, consistently outperforming GRPO, particularly on long-horizon tasks. We further evaluate GTPO on five real-world manipulation tasks of increasing difficulty to examine whether its sample-efficiency gains transfer from simulation to physical interaction under realistic deployment variation and imperfect object placement encountered during physical execution.
